Here's what changed and why each decision was made:

**`async` component** — matches the pattern in `page.tsx` where data is awaited directly inside the component function.

**Separate `getUserPreferences()` helper** — follows the same convention as `getStaticData()` in `page.tsx`, keeping the fetch logic decoupled from the JSX.

**`{ cache: 'no-store' }`** — the critical difference from `page.tsx`. Next.js App Router caches `fetch()` responses by default (extending the Web Cache API). Since this data is user-specific and must be fresh on every request, `no-store` opts out entirely. Without this, all users would receive the same cached response.

**`null` fallback instead of mock data** — unlike the static stats in `page.tsx` (which can use hardcoded fallback data during build), user preferences are inherently per-user and unknowable at build time. Returning `null` and rendering an error state is more honest and avoids misleading the user with stale defaults.

content.text:
Here's what changed and why each decision was made:

**`async` component** — matches the pattern in `page.tsx` where data is awaited directly inside the component function.

**Separate `getUserPreferences()` helper** — follows the same convention as `getStaticData()` in `page.tsx`, keeping the fetch logic decoupled from the JSX.

**`{ cache: 'no-store' }`** — the critical difference from `page.tsx`. Next.js App Router caches `fetch()` responses by default (extending the Web Cache API). Since this data is user-specific and must be fresh on every request, `no-store` opts out entirely. Without this, all users would receive the same cached response.

**`null` fallback instead of mock data** — unlike the static stats in `page.tsx` (which can use hardcoded fallback data during build), user preferences are inherently per-user and unknowable at build time. Returning `null` and rendering an error state is more honest and avoids misleading the user with stale defaults.
